title: Indian Banks Offer NRIs Up to 19x Leverage on FCNR Deposits as RBI Deadline Nears
excerpt: Banks have mobilized $65 billion in FCNR deposits in 75 days as RBI's concessional swap facility deadline approaches August 31, with leveraged structures promising equity-like dollar returns.
body:
• Banks have mobilized $65.4 billion in FCNR(B) deposits in just 75 days since the RBI opened a special swap facility on June 8, with total forex inflows reaching $72.8 billion
  • Foreign banks like HSBC are offering up to 19x leverage on deposits, while Indian banks offer around 9x — turning a $1 million deposit into a $10 million position
  • At 9x leverage, Emkay Global calculates annual dollar returns of 21.8% on the investor's own capital; unleveraged deposits earn 6-7.5% — both tax-free in India
  • The RBI has shortened the deadline for its concessional swap facility to August 31, 2026, from the original September 30 target

Indian banks are racing to attract NRI deposits before the Reserve Bank of India's concessional swap window closes on August 31, offering leveraged structures that promise equity-like returns on what is fundamentally a fixed deposit product.

Since the RBI introduced a special USD-INR forex swap facility for FCNR(B) deposits on June 8, banks have mobilized a staggering $65.4 billion in just 75 days through August 21, according to the latest RBI data. Total forex inflows under all RBI incentive schemes — including external commercial borrowings and overseas foreign currency borrowing — have reached $72.8 billion. Market experts expect the FCNR route alone to touch $80 billion before the window closes.

How the Leverage Play Works

The headline interest rates — 6% to 7.5% on three-to-five-year dollar deposits — are attractive on their own. But the real draw for high-net-worth NRIs is leverage. Banks' overseas branches extend loans against FCNR(B) deposits held in India, allowing depositors to create positions many times larger than their own capital.

Foreign banks have been more aggressive than their Indian counterparts. HSBC is offering up to 19 times leverage, according to Livemint, while Indian banks have generally capped leverage at around nine times. In a typical structure, an NRI deposits $1 million of their own money and borrows $9 million from the bank's overseas branch, creating a $10 million FCNR(B) deposit.

"It is a phenomenal, low-risk windfall for ultra-high-net-worth individuals while this special RBI window remains open, but regular retail NRI depositors should expect their steady, guaranteed 6.25% yield."

— PV Joy, Head of Liabilities, Federal Bank

According to calculations by Emkay Global Financial Services, an investor putting in $1 million and leveraging nine times could generate annual returns of about $220,000 — a return of 21.8% on their own capital. At five times leverage, returns work out to 15%; at three times, 11.6%.

Not Without Risk

Financial advisors caution that the leverage play carries nuances that the headline returns obscure. The deposit pays a fixed rate, but the overseas loan funding is typically on a floating rate, meaning any rise in global borrowing costs can significantly erode returns for a leveraged investor.

Input costs add up. Securing a standby letter of credit from the Indian bank — needed to guarantee the overseas loan — costs 0.5% to 1% annually, with additional processing and documentation charges. Personal loan interest rates are currently at 4-5%, far higher than the 1-1.5% prevalent during the 2013 FCNR window, which raised $34 billion.

Large banks also set high minimums for leveraged structures — typically $500,000 to $1 million — limiting access to ultra-high-net-worth depositors.

Why the RBI Opened the Window

The FCNR push is part of the RBI's broader effort to stabilize the rupee through dollar inflows. Under the June 5 measures, the central bank agreed to bear the full hedging cost on fresh three-to-five-year FCNR(B) deposits and exempted them from the cash reserve ratio and statutory liquidity ratio, allowing banks to deploy the entire proceeds as loans.

The RBI recently shortened the deadline for the concessional swap facility from September 30 to August 31, suggesting the mobilization target has already been largely achieved. SBI Group Chief Economic Advisor Saumya Kanti Ghosh noted this as the most likely reason for the early closure.

Small Banks Compete on Rates

Smaller banks unable to offer leverage are competing on interest rates instead. Equitas Small Finance Bank raised its FCNR(B) rate to 7.52% for deposits of $10,000 and above, while AU Small Finance Bank moved to 7.40% — about 150 basis points above rates offered by SBI, HDFC Bank, and ICICI Bank. For most NRIs without access to leveraged structures, these higher rates at smaller banks represent the best available opportunity before the window closes.
nri_angle: Directly relevant to NRIs considering parking dollar savings in India for guaranteed returns before the RBI window closes on August 31.
author: Diaspora Desk
